Read the full case study →
A guided fracture mechanics exercise. Learn how a slightly wavy crack front changes the stress intensity factors, first in tension and then in shear, and test the result with energy.

How do tough bands hold back a crack front under tension and shear?

A crack runs along a weak plane while it is pulled open and sheared at the same time. The plane is tougher in parallel bands, so the front is held back in each band and becomes wavy. How far does it lag, and how do the tension and the two shears change along it? The answer rests on one piece of mechanics: how the three stress intensity factors respond when the front is slightly curved. For tension this is a classical result, which you will meet first; then you will see what shear adds, and how an energy argument tests it.

You will practice
  • reading a nonlocal response: how the shape of the whole front changes the stress intensity factor at one point;
  • telling the two shear modes apart on a curved front, and seeing how the slope of the front couples them;
  • testing a response with a condition that comes from energy alone and needs no paper.
You need
  • the three modes of loading and the stress intensity factor;
  • the energy release rate, and Irwin’s relation between it and the stress intensity factors;
  • Fourier series of a periodic function, pen and paper, and a calculator.

New to fracture mechanics? Start with Fracture Mechanics 101; each step below links to the topic it needs, and the folds explain the working.

1 The problem

A crack lies in the plane y = 0 of an infinite, isotropic, linear elastic solid with Poisson's ratio 0.3. It covers the half-plane x < a(z) and can extend only within that plane, which is weak. Its front is the curve x = a(z). See the three modes of loading.

The solid is loaded from far away, and the loading does not change as the front moves: any straight front, wherever it lies, carries the same uniform stress intensity factors in tension and in the two shears, in the ratios 1 : 0.6 : 0.8. Along a curved front the two shear factors are taken in the local frame of the front, across it and along it.

The fracture energy of the weak plane varies along z only, with period λ: it is higher in bands centred at z = 0, ±λ, … and lower between them, with small contrast ε. The front is in equilibrium where the energy release rate equals the fracture energy at every point.

Left: the crack runs along a weak plane whose fracture energy is higher in periodic bands; in equilibrium the front lags in each band. Right: at each point of the front the loading has three parts, tension across the plane and shear along the local normal n and tangent t of the front, which turn with the slope of the front.

The model as given to the agents. The energy release rate is Irwin’s relation, with E Young’s modulus (see the energy release rate):

The loading is fixed by the stress intensity factors of a straight front:

The fracture energy of the weak plane varies along the front, with contrast ε and the profile g, which has zero mean and is largest at the band centres s = z/λ = 0, ±1, …:

The task has two parts. Part A is a warm-up with a prescribed front, a single cosine of small amplitude: report the cosine and sine coefficients of the three stress intensity factors and of G. Part B is the equilibrium front in the bands: the load level, the front shape and the three factors at sixteen points of a period, and the largest shear along the front with its position. Everything is asked to first order.

In Part B the front f and the changes κα of the stress intensity factors are counted per unit contrast ε; f is periodic with zero mean.

The task exactly as the AI agents received it

A crack front trapped by tough bands under mixed-mode loading

Solve the problem below and report the requested numbers in results.json. The problem is fully stated here; the method is your choice. Python 3 with NumPy and SciPy is available. Work only inside this folder.

1. The body and the crack

  • An infinite, homogeneous, isotropic, linear elastic solid with Young's modulus E and Poisson's ratio ν = 0.3. Small strains, quasi-static loading, no body forces.
  • Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z). A planar crack lies in the plane y = 0 and occupies the region x < a(z), where a(z) is a single-valued, smooth function. The crack front is the curve x = a(z), y = 0, which extends to z = ±∞. The crack faces are traction-free and do not touch.
  • The crack can extend only within the plane y = 0 (it runs along a weak plane of the solid).

Stress intensity factors. At a point of the front, let n be the unit vector normal to the front, lying in the plane y = 0 and pointing away from the crack (towards x > a), and let t = n × ey. For a straight front x = const this gives n = ex and t = ez. With σ the stress tensor evaluated in the plane y = 0 at distance r from the front along n, the stress intensity factors are

2 The physical picture

The picture shows the weak plane from above, as in Section 1, with the crack below the front and the unbroken plane above it. The front is the wavy front of Part A, drawn to scale:

The slider moves a point along one period of the front. At that point the arrows show the normal n and the tangent t of the front, and the dashed lines the frame of a straight front. The meters give the slope of the front there and the tension factor K1, from the classical result of step 1.

Slope of the front, a′:

Tension factor, K1/K10:

  1. Where the front lags, tension rises. A part of the front that lags behind its neighbours carries more tension than a straight front would, and a part that leads carries less. The change at one point depends on the shape of the whole front.
  2. A tough band holds the front back. In a band the front lags until the extra tension pays for the extra toughness. This is the trapping of Part B.
  3. Where the front tilts, its frame turns. On the flanks of a wave the normal and the tangent of the front turn with its slope. Part of the shear across the front becomes shear along it, and part of the shear along it becomes shear across it.
  4. Shear is not a copy of tension. The two shear modes respond to the shape of the front with their own weights, and the slope couples them in a way that is not a plain rotation. Steps 2 and 3 give both; step 4 tests them with energy.

From the case study:

Tension. Rice (1985) showed that a part of the front that lags behind its neighbours carries a higher K₁, and a part that leads carries a lower one. The change at a point depends on the whole front shape through a line operator 𝓛[a]; on a wavy front of wavenumber k it multiplies the wave by −|k|/2. This is why a tough band can hold a front back: the front lags there until the extra driving force balances the extra toughness.

3 Solve it step by step

Try each question, check your number, then open the working. Step 1 is the classical result for tension. Steps 2 and 3 add the two things shear brings: its own weights, and the coupling through the slope. Step 4 tests the shear terms with energy, and step 5 finds the front in the bands.

Step 1 Tension on a wavy front

Background: the stress intensity factor, mode I.

Move a short piece of a straight front forward: the tension factor falls at the piece and rises along the rest of the front, most near the piece. To first order the change is a line operator acting on the whole front shape a(z) (Rice 1985):

PV is the principal value of the integral at z′ = z. The operator compares the front at every z′ with the front at z: where the neighbours are ahead, the bracket is positive. For a loading whose straight-front factors do not depend on where the front lies, as here, the tension factor is

Your turn. For the cosine front of Part A, find the cosine coefficient of the tension factor. C1 =

Show the working

Why the operator multiplies a wave by −|k|/2: put a = cos kz and look at z = 0, with u = z′. The sine part of cos k(z + u) is odd in u and drops out of the integral, so the same holds at every z.

The front of Part A is a single cosine with k = 2π/λ; the constant ā does not enter the operator:

So C1 = −π ≈ −3.1416 and S1 = 0: tension responds to where the front is, not to its slope. At the troughs of the cosine the front lags and K1 is higher; at the crests it leads and K1 is lower. A shorter wave changes K1 more for the same amplitude, because the answer depends on A/λ.

Step 2 Shear has its own weights

Background: modes II and III.

On a straight front, shear across the front is mode II and shear along it is mode III. Gao and Rice (1986) found the first-order response of both on a slightly curved front (their Eq. 15). In the notation of this page it has two kinds of terms:

The weights p2 and p3 multiply the same operator as in tension. The couplings b2 and b3 multiply the slope a′ of the front; step 3 is about them. For tension the weight is 1. For shear the published weights are

Your turn. For the front of Part A, find the cosine coefficients of the two shear factors. C2 = C3 =

Show the working

The cosine terms come from the operator alone, as in step 1, now with the weight of each mode and the ratio of its straight-front factor to K10:

So C2 ≈ −1.2197 and C3 ≈ −3.4003. With the tension weight 1 for both, they would be −0.6π ≈ −1.8850 and −0.8π ≈ −2.5133.

Why two weights: the case’s note on the physics the runs missed puts it in one sentence.

Tension on a crack plane is a scalar problem with one compliance; shear is a vector problem with two, and a curved front mixes them.
Slip on a plane in an isotropic solid is resisted differently in two directions. Slip that varies along its own direction is edge-like (plane strain) and stiffer by the factor 1/(1 − ν) than slip that varies across its own direction, which is screw-like (anti-plane). […] A wavy front makes the fields vary along the front as well as across it, so mode 2 is no longer purely edge-like and mode 3 no longer purely screw-like.

Both weights are 1 at ν = 0, where the two directions are alike, and their mean is 1 at every ν. At ν = 0.3 they are 0.647 and 1.353: shear across the front responds to the waviness less strongly than tension, and shear along it more strongly.

Step 3 The slope couples the two shears

Background: the three modes, the local frame of the front.

The task measures K2 and K3 in the local frame of the front: across it, along the normal n, and along it, along the tangent t. Where the front is tilted by its slope a′, this frame turns. If the stress intensity factors simply turned with the frame, like the shear traction ahead of the front, the result would be a plain rotation:

That is b2 = b3 = 1. The published couplings reduce to this at ν = 0, and differ from it for ν > 0:

Your turn. For the front of Part A, find the sine coefficients of the two shear factors. S2 = S3 =

Show the working

The sine terms come from the slope alone. The slope of the cosine front is a sine, with a minus sign:

So S2 ≈ 5.9136 and S3 ≈ −3.1046. With the plain rotation they would be 2π(0.8) ≈ 5.0265 and −2π(0.6) ≈ −3.7699. The slope moves shear between the two modes only where there is shear to move: S2 needs K30, and S3 needs K20.

From the case study:

[T]he two shear modes are coupled through the local slope of the front: tilting the front turns part of each shear into the other […]. At ν = 0 these reduce to the plain rotation of the shear traction into the tilted frame; for ν > 0 they do not.

Step 4 The energy test

Background: the energy release rate.

The energy release rate G at a point of the front is the derivative of one elastic energy with respect to the position of the front there. Its first-order change is then a symmetric response: the change of G at z caused by moving the front at z′ equals the change at z′ caused by moving it at z, because a second derivative of one energy does not depend on the order. A term in the slope a′ breaks this: its parts of the two changes have opposite signs. So G may respond to where the front is, but not to its slope, and for the cosine front SG must be zero.

Expand Irwin’s relation to first order, with K32 weighted by m3 = 1/(1 − ν):

The slope terms of step 3 enter only through K2 and K3:

The two slope couplings must therefore stand in the ratio 1 − ν, whatever their source. The test needs no paper: any proposed response can be checked against it.

Your turn. Do the published couplings of step 3 pass? Compute their ratio. b3/b2 =

Your turn. Now test the plain rotation, b2 = b3 = 1. What sine coefficient of G does it give? SG =

Show the working

The published pair passes for every ν: b3/b2 = 1 − ν exactly, and SG = 0 for the task. The plain rotation fails for every ν > 0:

The rotation gives SG ≈ −1.1367: its energy release rate would depend on the slope of the front. The weights p2 and p3 do not enter SG; this test is about the couplings alone.

From the case study:

Energy. In the energy release rate the two slope terms cancel exactly. This is not an accident of the formulas. G is the derivative of one energy with respect to the position of the front, so the response of G to the front shape is a symmetric operator, and a term in the slope is antisymmetric. The condition fixes the ratio of the two slope couplings, b₃ = (1 − ν) b₂, whatever their source.

Step 5 The front held by the bands

Background: the energy release rate and the fracture energy.

With the slope terms gone, G responds to the front shape through the operator alone, like tension but with its own factor. Collect the cosine terms of steps 1 and 2 in the expansion of step 4:

Equilibrium, G = Γ at every point, has a mean part and a varying part. The mean part fixes the load level: G0 = Γ0. The varying part fixes the front.

Show the working

So ρ ≈ 0.9208 and CG ≈ −6.8237, against −2π ≈ −6.2832 for tension alone. Together the two shears restore a wavy front a little more strongly than tension does.

Your turn. Find the load level of Part B, and the height of the front from trough to crest. K10⁠√((1 − ν2)/EΓ0) = max f − min f =

Show the working

The load level is the mean part of G = Γ:

The varying part is one equation for the front, solved harmonic by harmonic. The toughness profile g is a sum of cosines with amplitudes 2qn, and the operator multiplies the n-th cosine by −πn/λ (step 1). Summing the series gives a logarithm:

The front lags most at the band centre, s = 0, and leads most midway between bands, s = 1/2:

So the load level is 0.6631 and the height is 0.3220ελ. Under tension alone, ρ = 1 and the height would be (ln 3)/π ≈ 0.3497ελ. Along the front the stress intensity factors follow from the response of steps 1 to 3:

κ1 follows the toughness. κ2 and κ3 also have a part from the slope, which is odd about the band centre; the explorer shows its effect.

From the case study:

The front shape is even about each band: it lags most at the band centre and leads most midway between bands, 0.322 ελ from trough to crest. Under tension alone the same bands would give 0.350 ελ. The shear loading of the task stiffens the front by the factor 1/ρ = 1.086, because the shear modes together restore a perturbed front more strongly than tension does.

The four requested numbers are C2 ≈ −1.2197 (step 2), S2 ≈ 5.9136 (step 3), SG = 0 (step 4) and max f − min f ≈ 0.3220 (this step). Enter them in the answer boxes.

5 Find the error

Three AI agents received the task without the paper and wrote down a first-order response of the three stress intensity factors. Each then solved the rest of the task correctly from its own response: its 76 numbers follow from its coefficients. The cards show the three responses, written in the notation of this page. In all three, K32 has the weight 1/(1 − ν) in G, as the task states.

Response A

Stated, with no source and no derivation.

Response B

Stated, and attributed to a paper.

Response C

Computed by the agent from the elasticity of the cracked solid.

None is zero: in each, b3/b2 differs from 1 − ν = 0.7. It is 0.8235 for A, 1 for B and 1.4286 for C.

Test 2 · the weights

Test 3 · the couplings

Compare the factors on the slope a′ in each card with the couplings of step 3, one at a time. A response can have one coupling right and the other wrong.

What happened

None of the three applied the energy test, and each fails it. A fourth agent, GPT-6.1 Sol, wrote down the published response, tested its slope terms at ν = 0 and required the sine term of G to vanish, and passed all 76 numbers.

Response A is Kimi K3.1 Pro, Response B is DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Response C is GLM-5.3, each in one run of the first round. Each agent ran once, in a container with Python, NumPy and SciPy, a three-hour limit and web tools off.

The case study, Section 10, describes the three runs as follows.

Kimi chose in its first sentence and never tested the choice. Its first message, written before any calculation, reads “I’ll use the coplanar first-order crack-front perturbation in Fourier space”. The form it then coded gives every mode the tension weight. […] The model can state the published result when asked (Section 6). Its files do not show missing knowledge. They show no step at which that knowledge was called on.
DeepSeek did not have the result and chose among guesses. Its first script compares four sign patterns of a tension-like term, each of magnitude one half: shear “unstable”, all modes “stable”, all “unstable”, and a mixed one. A second script scans six candidates. None has a weight that depends on Poisson's ratio. […]
GLM did the hard part and lost a sign. It spent two and a half hours computing the response from elasticity and obtained both shear weights. The sign of the coupling between the shear modes came out reversed. Its second way of reading the stress intensity factors disagreed with the first on exactly that coupling, and the run set the second aside (Section 8).
What none of the three did was test its response against something the response did not come from. The task offers one such test at no cost: the sine coefficient of G in Part A must be zero, because G cannot depend on the slope of the front. The three reported −0.47, −1.14 and −2.27.

These are the values you found in Test 1. The figure from the case study shows what the slope term does to the front: each dot is a value from a run’s saved answer.

Only one run's front lies on the reference; two are lopsided and one is reversed. Each dot is a value from a run's saved results file, at the sixteen points the task asks for; thin lines join the dots of one run. Top: three runs against the reference. A front that is not even about the band centre means that the run's energy release rate depends on the slope of the front. Bottom: the fourth run on a larger scale; its front leads in the tough band, where the reference lags. Counts are the points within the task's tolerance.

The case grades by piece of physics. Ten points go to each of seven pieces of the response, each tested by one or two numbers that isolate it, and 30 to the front and the stress intensity factors along it, counted only when the response is complete. GLM-5.3 (Response C) has 40 points, Kimi K3.1 Pro (A) 30 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (B) 20; of the 76 numbers they passed 8, 12 and 3. The rubric was written after the runs, at Teng Zhang's direction; the agents were told only that each number is compared with a reference. Each run’s method note and code were read by a second AI model, Grok 4.7, and by the authors of the case; no expert has reviewed it.

The case study, Section 10:

Close is not the same as right. Kimi's numbers are close: 63 of its 76 lie within ten times the tolerance, and its front is nowhere more than 0.021 ελ from the reference, whose height is 0.322 ελ. They are close because the errors in its two shear weights partly offset in the energy release rate at these load ratios (its net weight is 8% off), not because the physics is there, and they earn nothing.

In a second round, one sentence was added to the task: “Reminder. Carefully check the shear modes on the curved crack front.”

What the round shows. Each model reconsidered the shear modes, so the reminder was read. None answered it with the physics that was missing, and none tested that the energy release rate has no term in the slope. With one run per model in each round, the change in points (30 to 20, 20 to 20, 40 to 0) is not a rate.

6 Take away

Tension is not a template for shear

Two runs carried the tension response over to the shear modes, with the same weight or with its sign reversed. The published weights differ for each mode and depend on Poisson's ratio, and the shear modes are coupled through the slope, which tension is not. In this page: steps 2 and 3, and Responses A and B.

An energy has a symmetric response

G is the derivative of one energy with respect to the front position, so it cannot depend on the slope of the front at first order. All three failing answers have such a term, −0.47, −1.14 and −2.27 as the sine coefficient of G. One run saw it and explained it; the run that passed tested for it. In this page: step 4 and Test 1.

Residuals of your own equations do not test them

Kimi's eight checks pass near 10⁻¹⁵ and its answer scores 12 of 76. Each check re-evaluates the equations it started from. A check can only catch an error it does not share.

Two routes that disagree are the finding

GLM read the stress intensity factors from its solution in two ways. They disagreed on the coupling of the shear modes, the one quantity it got wrong. It resolved the disagreement by an argument that is not in its files, and reported the route it kept.

The four lessons are quoted from the case study; the line after the first two points to where this page uses them. They rest on a few runs of one problem. Treat them as ideas to test on new problems, not as measured error rates. The full case study also has the run that passed, the second round, the grading and what is established and what is not.
